title: Normalization in Neural Networks
description: How normalization keeps activations on a common scale to stabilize training, and how batch, layer, group, and instance normalization differ in what statistics they compute.
content:
**Normalization** in neural networks refers to a set of techniques that adjust the distribution of inputs or hidden activations to a common scale.

Normalization is crucial because it:
• Stabilizes and accelerates the training process
• Reduces sensitivity to parameter initialization
• Mitigates internal covariate shift - the phenomenon where the distribution of layer inputs changes during training

In practice, normalization can be applied to the input data or between layers. The common types differ mainly in which statistics they compute and over what they compute them.

**Batch normalization** operates on the activations of a layer by normalizing across the mini-batch. For each mini-batch during training, it computes the mean and variance of the activations and scales them so that they have roughly zero mean and unit variance. This speeds up convergence, allows for higher learning rates, and often reduces the need for dropout or other regularization techniques.

**Layer normalization** normalizes the activations across the features of each individual training example - statistics are calculated per sample rather than across samples. Its independence from batch size makes it ideal for sequential models such as RNNs and Transformers.

**Group normalization** strikes a balance between layer and batch normalization: it divides the channels of a layer into groups and computes normalization statistics within each group. It works consistently even when the mini-batch size is small.

**Instance normalization** normalizes each instance (sample) separately, and within each instance it normalizes each feature map (specifically in convolutional networks), treating each channel and each example independently. It is widely used in style transfer and generation applications, since it removes instance-specific contrast information, emphasizing content over style.

Quick summary:
• Batch - statistics across the mini-batch
• Layer - statistics per sample, across its features
• Group - statistics within groups of channels
• Instance - statistics per channel of each individual instance
